type_defs.exactMatch: the same concept; interchangeable in all contexts
type_defs.closeMatch: nearly the same; interchangeable in most contexts
type_defs.broadMatch: the candidate is broader (more general) than the source
type_defs.narrowMatch: the candidate is narrower (more specific) than the source
type_defs.relatedMatch: associated, but neither equivalent nor hierarchical

rules_html:
exactMatch
the same concept; interchangeable in all contexts
closeMatch
nearly the same; interchangeable in most contexts
broadMatch
the candidate is broader (more general) than the source
narrowMatch
the candidate is narrower (more specific) than the source
relatedMatch
associated, but neither equivalent nor hierarchical
none (reject)
no meaningful relationship
RULES for assigning match types:

1. SAME TYPE OF ENTITY. exactMatch, closeMatch, broadMatch and narrowMatch
   may only link two concepts that denote the SAME KIND of entity. When the
   two concepts are different kinds of thing, the strongest label allowed is
   relatedMatch. Example: "older generation" is NOT a closeMatch for "old
   age" — a generation is a group of people, whereas an age (or life stage)
   is not the same kind of entity — so they are at most relatedMatch.

2. narrowMatch (candidate narrower than the source) is valid only if the
   candidate is, with respect to the source, one of:
     (a) a specific TYPE of the source,
     (b) a PART or ELEMENT of the source, or
     (c) a specific INSTANCE of the source.

3. broadMatch (candidate broader than the source) applies the same three
   criteria in reverse: the SOURCE must be a type, part/element, or instance
   of the candidate.

4. Use relatedMatch for genuine but non-hierarchical or cross-type
   associations, and none when there is no useful relationship.

terms.label: demography
terms.gloss: Demography is the scientific study of human populations, focusing on their size, structure, and development.
terms.context:
Demography (101-1)  is the scientific study of human populations primarily with respect to their size, their structure (101-2) and their development; it takes into account the quantitative aspects of their general characteristics. It is the core of the population sciences (101-8), which in the broadest sense include interdisciplinary fields such as economic demography (104-1), social demography (104-2), population genetics (104-4), historical demography (102-1), mathematical demography (102-6) as well as contributions from the law, medicine, epidemiology (423-6), sociology, psychology, geography and philosophy. In statistical terminology any collection of distinct elements may be called a population (101-3), a word that is synonymous with universe (101-3). However, in demographic usage, the term population (101-4) refers to all of the inhabitants (101-5) of a given area, though on occasion it may be used for part of the inhabitants only [e.g., the school-age population (cf. 346-7), the marriageable population (cf. 514-2)]. Such groups are properly called sub-populations (101-6). The term population is often used to denote more specifically the size (101-7), i.e., the total number (101-7) of the aggregate referred to in no. 101-4.
 - 101-1  Demography, n. - demographic, adj. - demographer, n.: a specialist in demography.
 - 101-4  Population, n. - Note that this term may also be used adjectivally as a synonym for demographic, e.g., in population problems, population analysis, population studies.
 - 101-5  Inhabitant, n. - inhabit, v.: to occupy as a place of settled residence.

candidates.rationale: Both concepts refer to the scientific study of human populations.

terms.context: Certain sub-disciplines within demography have received special names reflecting their objectives or their methodology. Historical demography (102-1) deals with populations of the past for which written records are available. In the absence of such sources, the study of ancient populations takes the name of paleo-demography (102-2) . In descriptive demography (102-3) the numbers, geographical distribution, structure and change of human populations are described by means of population statistics (102-4) or demographic statistics (102-4) . The treatment of quantitative relations among demographic phenomena in abstraction from their association with other phenomena, is called theoretical demography (102-5) or pure demography (102-5) ; because of its resort to various mathematical methods, in practice it is identified with mathematical demography (102-6). A piece of research that applies the tools of demographic analysis (103-1) to an actual population is often called a demographic study (102-7). This study can focus on the current demographic situation (102-8) or current demographic conditions (102-8), i.e. the population change and its indicators during a short and recent period. All the preceding disciplines place a great emphasis on the numerical aspects of the phenomena, and are sometimes referred to as formal demography (102-9), when they apply only to the size and structure of the population. In contrast the broader term population studies (102-10) also includes the treatment of relations between demographic events and social, economic or other phenomena.

terms.label: demographic analysis
terms.gloss: Demographic analysis is the branch of formal demography that examines the effects of population size and structure on demographic processes.
terms.context:
Demographic analysis (103-1) is that branch of formal demography which controls for the effect of population size and structure on demographic processes (103-2) and isolates the effects of demographic processes of interest from the others, the latter of which are called competing processes (103-3). It also studies the relations between demographic variables and how they interact to form population structures. A distinction is made between cohort analysis (103-4) or generational analysis (103-4) which focuses on a well defined cohort (cf. 117-2) followed through time, and cross-sectional analysis (103-5) or period analysis (103-5) which focuses on the demographic phenomena that occur during a precise time interval (such as a calendar year) among several cohorts.

terms.label: economic demography
terms.gloss: Economic demography is the study of the relationships between demographic phenomena and economic factors.
terms.context:
The study of relations between demographic phenomena on one hand and economic and social phenomena on the other forms another branch of the subject. The terms economic demography (104-1) and social demography (104-2) have been used by some writers. Demography also deals with the study of population quality (104-3). This phrase may be used with reference to all sorts of social and personal characteristics. In a slightly different sense the term primarily refers to the distribution and transmission of hereditary characteristics (910-3) which are the subject of population genetics (104-4) . Human ecology (104-5) is the study of the distribution and organization of communities with attention to the operation of competitive and cooperative processes and has part of its subject matter in common with demography. Fields of research and methodology are even more intertwined in the case of demography and human geography (104-7). It is also the case for biometry (104-6) or biometrics (104-6) and epidemiology (104-8) which deal with the application of statistical methods to all forms of biological and medical research.
 - 104-4  Population genetics is distinct from human genetics, which deals with the transmission of inheritable characteristics in man: population genetics includes the study of the distribution and transmission of hereditary traits in plant, animal and human populations.
 - 104-5  Ecology, n. - ecological, adj. - ecologist, n.: a specialist in ecology.
 - 104-6  Biometry, n. - biometrics, n. - biometric, adj. - biometrician, n.: a specialist in biometry. The terms biostatistics, n. - biostatistical, adj. - and biostatistician, n. are frequently encountered and are synonymous with the terms given for biometry.

terms.label: statistical unit
terms.gloss: A fundamental unit used in demography for statistical analysis.
terms.context:
A fundamental statistical unit (110-1) used in demography is the individual (110-2) or person (110-2) . The term head (110-2) has also been employed but this usage is now largely out of date. The household (110-3), a socio-economic unit, consists of individuals who live together. Statistical definitions of the household vary. According to the definition which has been recommended as an international standard a household consists of a group of individuals who share living quarters (120-1) and their principal meals. The term hearth (110-3) has been used in the past, showing that in the past members of the household used to share the same fire. Classifications of households also vary between different countries and different enquiries. Most classifications involve the distinction of two types: private households (110-4) and collective households (110-5) . An individual living by himself is considered to be a one-person household (110-6) . A boarder (110-7) is a person other than a domestic servant, who is unrelated to other members of the household and who habitually takes his meals with the household. A lodger (110-8) or roomer (110-8), on the other hand, does not habitually take his meals with the household. These two categories may or may not be included in the household for statistical purposes.
 - 110-4  Private households are called family households when their members are related.
 - 110-5  Collective  households may include institutional households composed of persons who reside in specifically designated institutions (e.g. hospitals, prisons, etc.). They may also include unrelated persons who reside in group quarters (120-1) other than institutions. However, recent internationally recommended definitions restrict the terms household and household population to private households, and refer otherwise to persons not living in households.

terms.label: one-person household
terms.gloss: A household consisting of a single individual living alone.
terms.context:
A fundamental statistical unit (110-1) used in demography is the individual (110-2) or person (110-2) . The term head (110-2) has also been employed but this usage is now largely out of date. The household (110-3), a socio-economic unit, consists of individuals who live together. Statistical definitions of the household vary. According to the definition which has been recommended as an international standard a household consists of a group of individuals who share living quarters (120-1) and their principal meals. The term hearth (110-3) has been used in the past, showing that in the past members of the household used to share the same fire. Classifications of households also vary between different countries and different enquiries. Most classifications involve the distinction of two types: private households (110-4) and collective households (110-5) . An individual living by himself is considered to be a one-person household (110-6) . A boarder (110-7) is a person other than a domestic servant, who is unrelated to other members of the household and who habitually takes his meals with the household. A lodger (110-8) or roomer (110-8), on the other hand, does not habitually take his meals with the household. These two categories may or may not be included in the household for statistical purposes.
 - 110-4  Private households are called family households when their members are related.
 - 110-5  Collective  households may include institutional households composed of persons who reside in specifically designated institutions (e.g. hospitals, prisons, etc.). They may also include unrelated persons who reside in group quarters (120-1) other than institutions. However, recent internationally recommended definitions restrict the terms household and household population to private households, and refer otherwise to persons not living in households.

terms.label: member of the household
terms.gloss: A member of the household is an individual who resides in a private household.
terms.context:
When a private household (110-4) contains several persons they are called members of the household (111-1) and one of them will be the head of the household (111-2). There is no universally accepted rule as to who is considered the head of the household; in some cases it may be the principal earner (111-3). On most census schedules there appears a question dealing with the relationship (111-4) (114-3) of members of the household to its head. This enables a distinction to be made between different groups in composite households (111-5) or complex households (111-5) which contain members of more than one biological family or nuclear family (113-1). A composite or complex household can be disaggregated into several nuclei (111-6), including a primary nucleus (111-7) and secondary nuclei (111-8). The nuclei are more commonly called families (112-1). The primary family (111-9) is that of the household head when it is defined, the others are called secondary families (111-10). Household size (111-11) denotes the number of persons included in the household.
 - 111-2  The term householder is sometimes used to refer to the head of the household. The term headship is frequently encountered.
 - 111-6  The nucleus is also called a conjugal family unit.

terms.label: generation
terms.gloss: A generation refers to a group of persons born within a specified period of time, generally taken as a calendar year.
terms.context:
In demographic literature, the term generation (116-1) has been given a precise meaning and refers to a group of persons born within a specified period of time, generally taken as a calendar year. The term cohort (116-2) denotes a group of persons who experience a certain event in a specified period of time: thus birth cohort is a synonym for generation in the sense of 116-1, a marriage cohort is a group of persons married within a defined period, etc. In demography as in genealogy the term generation (116-3) may also be used to denote the descendants of a group of persons who are themselves a generation in the sense of 116-1. Thus the children of a group of migrants are often referred to as the second generation (116-9). Occasionally we also use the expression third or fourth generation. Generations can be qualified according to their current age as, for example, the young and rising generation (116-6), the middle-aged generation (116-7) or the generation in the prime of life (116-7) and the older generation (116-8) while the age limits are often vague and therefore require clarification. Cohorts of people born during historical periods related to low birth rates (or high) can be referred as birth-dearth or low-birth-rate cohorts (116-11) (or high-birth-rate cohorts (116-10)--more colloquially baby-boomers). Occasionally consideration is restricted to lines of descent through one sex only, thus a male generation (116-4) or paternal generation (116-4) are the sons of a generation of males, a female generation (116-5) or maternal generation (116-5) the daughters of a generation of females. These distinctions are normally used when the length of a generation or mean interval between successive generations is calculated. (cf. 713-1). - 116-2 Cohort, n.: the term cohort analysis is used to denote a method of analyzing data, in which the experience of individual cohorts is studied throughout their lives, or other specified periods.
For purposes of military service the number of men who become liable to conscription in a given year is sometimes called the class of that year. In the United States the same term is used for a group of students who complete their studies at a particular school or university in a particular year. - 116-11 Because of the depletion of births during the First World war, particularly in France, the French term “classes creuses” is sometimes used in the literature.

terms.label: cohort
terms.gloss: A cohort denotes a group of persons who experience a certain event in a specified period of time.
terms.context:
In demographic literature, the term generation (116-1) has been given a precise meaning and refers to a group of persons born within a specified period of time, generally taken as a calendar year. The term cohort (116-2) denotes a group of persons who experience a certain event in a specified period of time: thus birth cohort is a synonym for generation in the sense of 116-1, a marriage cohort is a group of persons married within a defined period, etc. In demography as in genealogy the term generation (116-3) may also be used to denote the descendants of a group of persons who are themselves a generation in the sense of 116-1. Thus the children of a group of migrants are often referred to as the second generation (116-9). Occasionally we also use the expression third or fourth generation. Generations can be qualified according to their current age as, for example, the young and rising generation (116-6), the middle-aged generation (116-7) or the generation in the prime of life (116-7) and the older generation (116-8) while the age limits are often vague and therefore require clarification. Cohorts of people born during historical periods related to low birth rates (or high) can be referred as birth-dearth or low-birth-rate cohorts (116-11) (or high-birth-rate cohorts (116-10)--more colloquially baby-boomers). Occasionally consideration is restricted to lines of descent through one sex only, thus a male generation (116-4) or paternal generation (116-4) are the sons of a generation of males, a female generation (116-5) or maternal generation (116-5) the daughters of a generation of females. These distinctions are normally used when the length of a generation or mean interval between successive generations is calculated. (cf. 713-1). - 116-2 Cohort, n.: the term cohort analysis is used to denote a method of analyzing data, in which the experience of individual cohorts is studied throughout their lives, or other specified periods.
For purposes of military service the number of men who become liable to conscription in a given year is sometimes called the class of that year. In the United States the same term is used for a group of students who complete their studies at a particular school or university in a particular year. - 116-11 Because of the depletion of births during the First World war, particularly in France, the French term “classes creuses” is sometimes used in the literature.

terms.label: specific ratio
terms.gloss: A specific ratio is a comparison of quantities of the same kind but from different categories, such as men and women.
terms.context:
One of the first stages of analysis (132-1) consists of relating the population totals or number of events to other totals or numbers. The resulting indices are given various names. A ratio (133-6), also used for various purposes, is the quotient obtained by dividing quantities of the same kind. When the dividend and divisor belong to the same kind but different categories (men and women, children and women, different age-groups, for example) an other terminology might be used in non English languages, relating both quantities with a specific ratio (133-1) (like a sex ratio). A proportion (133-2) is a ratio which indicates the relation in magnitude of a part to the whole. A percentage (133-3) is a proportion expressed per hundred. A rate (133-4) is a special type of ratio used to indicate the relative frequency (133-5) of the occurrence of a particular event within a population or a sub-population in a specified period of time, usually one year. Although this usage is recommended, the term has steadily acquired a wider meaning and is often incorrectly used as a synonym for ratio (e.g. labor force participation rate, which is actually a proportion).

Some rates, however, are given per ten thousand, per one hundred thousand, or per million e.g. cause-specific death rates (421-10). On other occasions rates may be given per person or per hundred. terms.label: intensity
terms.gloss: Intensity refers to the measure of how frequently a demographic phenomenon occurs within a specified cohort.
terms.context:
The primary objective of cohort analysis (103-4) is the study of the intensity (138-1) and tempo (138-2) or timing (138-2) of demographic phenomena. The intensity of a phenomenon initiated by one non-renewable event (201-4) may be measured by either the ultimate frequency (138-3) of occurrence for the given event or by its complement. The ultimate frequency reflects the proportion of persons who would have experienced the event, in the absence of extraneous influences, during the existence of the cohort (116-2). The intensity of a phenomenon initiated by a renewable event (201-5) such as births or migratory moves, can be measured by the mean number of events (138-4) per person in the cohort, also in the absence of extraneous influences. Tempo or timing may be defined as the distribution over time within the cohort of the demographic events corresponding to the investigated phenomenon. The results of cross-sectional analysis or period analysis (103-5) are summarized by period measures (138-5) — as opposed to cohort measures (138-6) — which can be constructed in various fashions. A commonly used technique consists in attributing the observed rates pertaining to various ages or durations to a hypothetical cohort (138-7) or synthetic cohort (138-7) .
 - 138-3  This ultimate frequency or its complement has received various names according to the phenomenon studied: parity progression ratio (637-7), frequency of definitive celibacy (521-1) ... It is best not to use the word proportion as part of these names, and to reserve it for observed proportions. For instance, the frequency of definitive celibacy must be kept distinct from the proportion single at a given age, as recorded in a census.
 - 138-4  It is not unusual to give the same name to the observed mean number of events per person, and to the number that would have been observed in the absence of extraneous influences such as mortality. Distinct phrases should be used; for instance, the number of children ever born (637-2) can be distinguished from cumulative fertility (636-2). 
 - 138-5  Because cross-sectional analysis and hypothetical cohorts were used before genuine cohort analysis, the names of period indices often seem to imply that they refer to a cohort. This usage may lead to apparent contradictions. For example, parity-specific birth probabilities may exceed one for certain years when many postponed births are made up.

terms.label: time series
terms.gloss: A demographic time series is a sequence of values of a demographic variable recorded over time.
terms.context:
When values of a demographic variable are available over time, a demographic time series (150-1) is obtained. It is sometimes possible to decompose a time series into a trend (150-2) around which there are fluctuations (150-3), variations (150-3), or deviations (150-3) (141-2). Where such fluctuations tend to recur after certain periods, usually several years, they are called cyclical fluctuations (150-4) or, more generally, period fluctuations (150-4). In demography the most common period for compiling data is a year, and the fluctuations in sub-periods of a year are called seasonal fluctuations (150-5). The fluctuations that remain after trend, cyclical, and seasonal fluctuations have been eliminated are called irregular fluctuations (150-6). They may be due to exceptional factors such as wartime mobilization, or sometimes they are chance fluctuations (150-7) or random fluctuations (150-7).

terms.label: smoothing
terms.gloss: Graduation or smoothing is the process of replacing a series of figures with another series that shows greater regularity.
terms.context:
It is occasionally desirable to replace a series of figures by another series that shows greater regularity. This process is known as graduation (151-1) or smoothing (151-1), and it generally consists of passing a smooth curve through a number of points in the time series or other series, such as the number of persons distributed by reported age. If a free-hand curve is drawn the process is called graphic graduation (151-2). When analytical mathematical methods are used, this is called curve fitting (151-3). A mathematical curve is fitted to the data, possibly by the method of least squares (151-4), which minimizes the sum of the squares of the differences between the original and the graduated series. Other methods include moving averages (151-5) or involve the use of the calculus of finite differences (151-6). Some of these procedures may be used for interpolation (151-7), the estimation of values of the series at points intermediate between given values, or for extrapolation (151-8), the estimation of values outside of the range for which it was given.

terms.label: interpolation
terms.gloss: Interpolation is the estimation of values of a series at points that are intermediate between given values.
terms.context:
It is occasionally desirable to replace a series of figures by another series that shows greater regularity. This process is known as graduation (151-1) or smoothing (151-1), and it generally consists of passing a smooth curve through a number of points in the time series or other series, such as the number of persons distributed by reported age. If a free-hand curve is drawn the process is called graphic graduation (151-2). When analytical mathematical methods are used, this is called curve fitting (151-3). A mathematical curve is fitted to the data, possibly by the method of least squares (151-4), which minimizes the sum of the squares of the differences between the original and the graduated series. Other methods include moving averages (151-5) or involve the use of the calculus of finite differences (151-6). Some of these procedures may be used for interpolation (151-7), the estimation of values of the series at points intermediate between given values, or for extrapolation (151-8), the estimation of values outside of the range for which it was given.

terms.label: forecast table
terms.gloss: A forecast table provides numerical values of demographic functions that can be used for population forecasting.
terms.context: The numerical values of demographic functions are generally listed in tables (153-1), such as life tables (431-1), fertility tables (634-1), or nuptiality tables (522-1). A distinction is usually made between calendar-year tables (153-2) or period tables (153-2) which are based upon observations collected during a limited period of time, and cohort tables (153-3) or generation tables (153-3) which deal with the experience of a cohort throughout its lifetime. A multiple decrement table (153-4) illustrates the simultaneous effects of several non-renewable events, such as the effects of first marriage and death on the single population. The most used are double decrement tables (153-4). Forecast tables (153-5) provide numerical values of demographic functions, like survival functions (431-6) for example, which can be used directly for population forecast (cf. 720-2). When a population is classified in two or more categories according to age, like economic status (women in the labor force or out of the labor force, for example), marital statuses, regions etc. and when continuous flows between categories are possible over time even if the individual state can usually be measured only at discrete times (waves of a longitudinal study, queries to population registers etc.), increment-decrement methods (153-6) or multi-state methods (153-6) are more appropriate.

terms.label: current population statistics
terms.gloss: Current population statistics refer to the static aspects of a population, providing an instantaneous snapshot at a specific moment in time.
terms.context: Current population statistics (201-1) may be distinguished from statistics of population change (201-2). They deal with the static aspects of the subject and give an instantaneous picture of the population at a given moment of time: the statistical units (110-1) used are generally households (110-3), individuals (110-2), etc. Statistics of population change are concerned with the continuous processes of change which affect a population, and deal largely with vital events (201-3),such as births, marriages, deaths, and with migration (801-1). Nonrenewable events (201-4) (e.g. deaths) may be distinguished from renewable events (201-5) such as pregnancies, births or migratory moves; renewable events are assigned an order (201-6) based on the number of previous events of the same nature for the same person. Statistics of population change are a principal source for the study of population processes (201-7), sometimes called population dynamics (201-7). Censuses (cf. 202) are the main source of information on the state of the population (201-8) . Vital Statistics (212-1) are the primary source of data for the study of population growth (201-9) (cf. 701). Occasionally they deal with natural increase (201-10) only, i.e. they do not take into account movement between the population studied and other populations, but logically migration statistics (812-1) are a part of the statistics of population change. The term population movement (201-11) is used to refer to the geographical movement of a population.

terms.label: enumeration
terms.gloss: An enumeration is an operation designed to yield a total population count.
terms.context:
An enumeration (203-1) is any operation which is designed to yield a population total. It differs from a simple count (203-2) in that a list (203-3) is generally prepared. An inquiry (203-4) or survey (203-4) on the other hand, is generally an operation which is designed to furnish information on a special subject (e.g. the labor force) and which has limited aims. A field inquiry (203-5) or field survey (203-5) is an inquiry in which information is obtained by personal interview (203-6). In postal inquiries (203-7) or mailback surveys (203-7) questionnaires (206-3) are sent out by post with a request to return them completed. A retrospective survey (203-8) focuses on past demographic events; in a multiround survey (203-9) those events that occurred since the previous survey are noted from the second round on. This type of survey should not be confused with a call back (203-10), a term used to describe the instance where the interviewer is obliged to make several attempts to reach a respondent. In censuses, information may be obtained by either direct interview (203-11), or by self-enumeration (203-12). In the first method, also called canvasser method (203-11) the enumerator (204-2) notes the information provided by or about the respondents; in the second method, also called householder method (203-12), the questionnaire is completed by the respondents (204-1) themselves. Self-enumeration may take the form of a mail census (203-13).
 - 203-1  Enumeration, n. - enumerate, v.
 - 203-2  Count, n. - count, v.
 - 203-3  List, n. - list, v.
 - 203-4  Survey, n. - survey, v.

terms.label: de jure population
terms.gloss: The resident population, or de jure population, consists of the people who habitually live in a given area.

In the resident population, temporary absentees (310-4) are included with those permanent residents (310-3) who are present in the area on census day; the actual population consists of residents together with visitors (310-5) or transients (310-5). The two methods of enumeration will give different results even for the country as a whole. The place where a person lives is called the place of residence (310-6). For administrative reasons, certain persons who live together in large communities (i.e. boarding schools, military persons in barracks, prisoners, etc. (cf. 110-5) are often separately enumerated. These persons form the institutional population (310-7). Special rules are used to enumerate homeless (310-8) or persons of no fixed abode (310-8).

terms.label: age
terms.gloss: Age is a fundamental characteristic of population structure, typically expressed in years or months.
terms.context:
Age (322-1) is another fundamental characteristic of population structure. Generally it is expressed in years, or years and months; in the case of very small children, it may be given in months and days, or in years and decimal fractions of years. Demographers usually truncate the age to the number of complete years (322-2) lived, and this is called age at last birthday (322-3). Occasionally demographic statistics refer to the age reached during the year (322-4). Where the fraction of the last complete year lived is counted as a whole year, as in some actuarial applications, we speak of age at next birthday (322-5). Stated age (322-6) or reported age (322-6), in a census or vital registration, is often rounded upward to the next integer especially when the next birthday is near. The term exact age (322-7) is used, particularly in life table calculations, to denote the time when an individual reaches his birthday. Census questions include either the date of birth, age at last birthday, or even simply age without further precision. When the knowledge of ages is not widespread, a historical calendar (322-8) may be used to estimate ages. This is a list of events with a known date that occurred during the lifetime of the respondents.
 - 322-2  Thus, age groups (325-2) are usually expressed in completed years and the group aged 6-13 years includes the individuals whose exact ages (322-7) are comprised between 6 and 14 years.

terms.context: Inhabitants of a nation or state may be subjects (330-1) citizens (330-1) or nationals (330-1) of that state, who enjoy certain political rights, or they may be aliens (330-2) or foreigners (330-2) who are citizens of another state, or citizens of no state at all and called stateless (330-3). The term “subject” used to have a servile connotation but has tended to lose it and is frequently taken as a synonym of citizen, though occasionally a distinction is made between a subject and a citizen. Citizens of a state generally possess the nationality (330-4) of that state. This term is nowadays used as a synonym for citizenship (330-4), but in some multi-national states (330-6) a distinction may be drawn between political nationality (330-4) and ethnic nationality (330-5).

candidates.elsst_def: NATIONAL ORIGIN; THE FACT OF BELONGING TO A PARTICULAR NATION; THE LEGAL RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE SUBJECT AND THE STATE
candidates.rationale: Nationality and political nationality are nearly the same, both involving legal status and belonging to a state.

Educational attainment statistics (342-4) classify individuals by grade attainment (342-5), years of school completed (342-5) or, more rarely, by age at leaving school (342-6). Another type of classification is based upon the diploma (342-7), degree (342-7) or certificate (342-7) obtained, and depends on the organization of instruction (342-8) in each country.
 - 342-2  Literate, adj. - literacy, n. Literacy statistics are the part of education statistics that refer to the ability to read and write. The literacy ratio is the proportion of the population covered that is literate. Its complement is the illiteracy ratio.
 - 342-3  Illiterate, adj. - illiteracy, n. A person who is able to read but not write may be called semi-literate, and such persons are sometimes classed with the literate and at other times with the illiterate population.
 - 342-4  The school-age population (346-7) is often classifed by grade or level of enrollment, and attainment is then presented only for the population beyond normal school age.

terms.label: leaving school
terms.gloss: Leaving school refers to the act of a student exiting the educational system before completing their studies, which is uncommon during the compulsory education period.
terms.context: Other statistics concern educational progression. An individual progresses normally grade by grade, from the lowest class of elementary school, to the end of his studies. Leaving school (347-1), where compulsory education is enforced, is exceptional during school age, barring illness or death. The dropout rate (347-2) is the probability of leaving school before obtaining a degree, either during the year or at the end of a grade, and it is constructed in the same way as a probability of dying in a life table; its complement to one is the retention rate (347-3). Such rates can be used to compute a table of school life (347-4), from which it is possible to infer the mean length of schooling (347-5). At the end of the school year, pupils or students who do not terminate their studies, may either repeat the grade or move on to the next grade, with or without change of track (347-6). According to the fate of these pupils or students at the end of the academic year, proportion repeating a school year (347-7) are established.

terms.label: economically active population
terms.gloss: The economically active population consists of individuals engaged in gainful activities.
terms.context:
A distinction is generally made between the working population (350-1) or economically active population (350-1) and the unoccupied population (350-2) or economically inactive population (350-2). Generally speaking, the working population consists of those individuals engaged in gainful activities (350-3). A gainful activity, or economic activity (350-3), is an activity which contributes to the production of income. Unpaid family workers (353-5) are usually included in the economically active population. Homemakers (350-4) or housewives (350-4) engaged in unpaid domestic duties, students, retired workers, etc. are usually excluded. The members of the economically inactive population are sometimes referred to as dependents (350-5) (358-1) in the sense that they subsist on the product of the working population. (See, however, the different sense of this term stated in § 358). The ratio of the working population to the total population, usually computed with reference to a given sex-age group or other category, is called the activity ratio (350-6) or labor force participation ratio (350-6). - 350-1 The terms gainfully occupied population, gainful workers, labor force are used as synonyms for working population and economically active population.
For statistical measurement of the working population, the gainful worker concept or the labor force concept may be used. According to the gainful worker concept, the working population is defined as being composed of those persons who have a gainful activity which they normally exercise. According to the labor force concept, it is defined as the group of persons who were working at a gainful occupation or wanting or seeking such work during a specified period preceding the inquiry.

terms.label: worker
terms.gloss: Workers are individuals who make up the working population.
terms.context:
Workers (351-1) who make up the working population can be classified as employed (351-2) or unemployed (351-3). Under the labor force concept (350-1 ), only persons who were actively seeking work (351-4) or are on temporary layoff during the specified period are usually counted as unemployed. It is important to distinguish between persons who have never had a job and persons who are looking for their first job (351-11) or first-time job seekers (351-11). The employed population (351-5) consists of all those currently working for pay or profit. Among the economically active, a substantial portion of workers may be compelled by the economic conditions of the country or of the time, to perform less work than they would normally be able and willing to perform; in this instance, the terms underemployment (351-6) or partial employment (351-6) are used. Marginal workers (351-7) who only very occasionally participate in economic activity, are most often classified as not in the labor force under the gainful worker concept (350-1 ). The employment to population ratio (351-8) is the proportion of employed persons in the working age group (usually 15 to 64). Inactive persons (351-9) are those who do not accomplish any kind of professional activity neither are looking for any employment.  Hidden unemployment (351-10) or labor reserve (351-10)  includes people who, although not officially registered as unemployed, are looking for a private work as well as those who do not exercise nor are looking for a job but if some job opportunities arose to them, could respond.

terms.label: marginal worker
terms.gloss: Marginal workers are individuals who occasionally participate in economic activity and are often classified as not in the labor force.
terms.context:
Workers (351-1) who make up the working population can be classified as employed (351-2) or unemployed (351-3). Under the labor force concept (350-1 ), only persons who were actively seeking work (351-4) or are on temporary layoff during the specified period are usually counted as unemployed. It is important to distinguish between persons who have never had a job and persons who are looking for their first job (351-11) or first-time job seekers (351-11). The employed population (351-5) consists of all those currently working for pay or profit. Among the economically active, a substantial portion of workers may be compelled by the economic conditions of the country or of the time, to perform less work than they would normally be able and willing to perform; in this instance, the terms underemployment (351-6) or partial employment (351-6) are used. Marginal workers (351-7) who only very occasionally participate in economic activity, are most often classified as not in the labor force under the gainful worker concept (350-1 ). The employment to population ratio (351-8) is the proportion of employed persons in the working age group (usually 15 to 64). Inactive persons (351-9) are those who do not accomplish any kind of professional activity neither are looking for any employment.  Hidden unemployment (351-10) or labor reserve (351-10)  includes people who, although not officially registered as unemployed, are looking for a private work as well as those who do not exercise nor are looking for a job but if some job opportunities arose to them, could respond.

terms.label: employee

terms.context:

A combination of occupational and status classifications may be used to construct social status categories (353-6).

terms.label: mortality
terms.gloss: Mortality refers to the study of the effect of death on the population.
terms.context:
The study of mortality (401-1) deals with the effect of death on the population. The general terms mortality rate (401-2) or death rate (401-2) encompass all the rates (133-4) which measure the frequency of deaths (401-3). Where the expression death rate is used without any qualifying adjective the crude death rate (401-4) is usually meant (cf. 136-8 for a general discussion of crude rates). This is generally an annual rate and consists of the ratio of the annual number of deaths occurring during a calendar year to the number exposed to the risk of dying during the same period. This number is equivalent to the mean population (401-5) or average population (401-5) for the period, and the population at the mid-point of the period can usually be substituted for the average population without appreciable error, if the size of the population is changing fairly uniformly. If the mortality of a sub-population (101-6) only is studied, we speak of specific death rates (134-6) among which sex-age-specific death rates (401-6) are the most common. Age specific death rates (401-7) without distinction of sex are also used on occasion.
 - 401-2  Occasionally the term mortality is used as a synonym for mortality rate or death rate.
 - 401-3  Death, n. - die, v. - dead, adj. syn. - deceased, adj. or n.
 - 401-5  When the observation period exceeds one year, the mean population is generally obtained as the average of several estimates of the size of the population for each year. The average number of persons years (135-6) is also used as denominator.

terms.label: mortality in utero
terms.gloss: Mortality in utero refers to deaths that occur prior to the complete expulsion or extraction of a product of conception from its mother.

Early foetal mortality (411-3) occurs before the twentieth week of gestational life, while intermediate foetal mortality (411-4) occurs between the twentieth and the 28th week of gestation. After the twenty-eighth week, one refers to late foetal mortality (411-5) and the product is called a late foetal death (411-5) or, popularly, a stillbirth (411-5). Perinatal mortality (411-6) includes late foetal mortality and a portion of infant mortality that may include either early neo-natal deaths, or all neo-natal deaths. The foeto-infant mortality (411-7) includes stillbirths and deaths of children under one year.

terms.label: intra-uterine mortality table

terms.context:

These indices greatly understate intra-uterine mortality since early intra-uterine deaths frequently remain unobserved or unknown. A better measurement of intra-uterine mortality is provided by intra-uterine mortality tables (413-5), a specialized application of the life table (cf. 432) which takes into account the duration of gestation. The perinatal mortality rate (413-6) relates perinatal deaths (411-6) to the sum of late foetal deaths and live births. The foeto-infant death rate (413-7) represents the number of known stillbirths and deaths in the first year of life per one thousand live births and stillbirths of the same reporting period.

An endemic disease (423-1) is one that permanently affects substantial segments of a population, in contrast with an epidemic (423-2), which spreads and then disappears within a fairly short time; when it appears in a large number of countries, it is called a pandemic (423-3). A distinction is sometimes made between chronic diseases (423-8) and acute diseases (423-9). These terms are not precisely defined, but acute diseases are generally understood to be those of abrupt onset and short duration while chronic diseases are those with slow onset and long duration, and often causing prolonged disability.

terms.label: endogenous mortality
terms.gloss: Endogenous mortality refers to death resulting from the genetic constitution of the individual.

Demographers devote particular attention to certain aspects of mortality: endogenous mortality (424-1) which results from the genetic constitution of the individual, congenital malformations (424-2), injuries connected with birth, or degenerative diseases associated with aging; exogenous mortality (424-3), in contrast, results from external causes such as infectious or parasitic diseases and accidental injuries other than those incurred by the child during birth. Mortality from these latter diseases is called maternal mortality (424-5), and a maternal death rate (424-6) may be computed as the ratio of maternal deaths in a year to the births of the same year. terms.label: morbidity rate
terms.gloss: Morbidity rate is a measure of the frequency or occurrence of illness within a population.
terms.context:
Three aspects of morbidity (420-1) are commonly measured by morbidity rates (425-1) or morbidity ratios (425-1): frequency, duration and severity. These indices may be computed for specific diseases, or for all diseases. Two indices of the frequency of ill-health are the incidence rate (425-2), the number of new cases of disease during the period related to the average population, and the prevalence rate (425-3), the number of cases existing at a given moment of time expressed per unit of the average population. Either the average duration per case (425-4), or the disability rate (425-5), which is the mean number of days of illness (425-5) per person in the population, may serve as a measure of the duration of illness. The case fatality rate (425-6), which is the proportion of fatal cases among the reported cases of the specified diseases, may be used as an index of severity.
 - 425-5  Disability rate is an inappropriate, but commonly used, term for a ratio of the number of days lived with illness divided by the number of days lived by the entire population, both in the same time interval.
 - 425-6  This is said to measure the lethality of the disease.

terms.context: Probabilities of dying (431-1) or death probabilities (431-1) are used to study in detail the mortality of a period or of a cohort. If n = 1, we talk about annual death probabilities (431-2); if n = 5, about quinquennial death probabilities (431-3). The instantaneous death rate (431-4), or as it is occasionally called the force of mortality (431-4), is the limit of the nqx value as n tends to zero. The projective mortality probability (431-5) is the probability that individuals of the same cohort or group of cohorts died between two January 1st). The name of this probability comes from its use in the calculation of population projections. It is also equal to 1-Lx+n/Lx, where Lx is the person-years lived by the stationary population from exact age x to exact age x+n. The complement to one of the probability of dying from exact age x to exact age x + n is the probability of survival (431-6) over this interval. In the preparation of population projections, we use survival ratios (431-7); they represent the probability that individuals of the same birth cohort or group of cohorts will still be alive n years later. - 431-1 The probability of death between age x and x + n is defined as the ratio of deaths between ages x and x+n to the number of survivors at exact age x. It is not to be confused with the central death rate, the ratio of deaths between ages x and x+n to the mean population alive at that age. The central death rate is written nmx . - 431-6 The probability of survival from age x to age x+n is written npx . - 431-7 A survival ratio is the complement to one of the projective mortality probability. A person who is married to several persons simultaneously is called polygamous (502-4). A distinction is made between polyandrous (502-5) societies, where a woman may have several husbands, and polygynous (502-6) societies, where a man may have several wives. The term "polygamy" is frequently used in the sense of polygyny.

terms.label: civil marriage
terms.gloss: A civil marriage is a legal union established through a ceremony performed by a state official.
terms.context:
In some countries a legal union can be established only through a civil marriage (503-1) performed by an official of the state; in other countries a religious marriage (503-2) in accordance with the regulations of a church is recognized as having legal force. Social or legal recognition may be given under various conditions in different countries to stable unions which have not been solemnized by a legal or religious ceremony, for instance to customary marriages (503-3) or to common law marriages (503-3) conforming to local traditions. Different types of relationships and degrees of social acceptance are implied in terms applied to various unions but their significance varies widely in different countries. The term consensual union (503-4) implies a socially recognized stable union, the term companionate marriage (503-4) has a similar connotation. The terms free union (503-5) and temporary union (503-6) both imply a less stable union that may or may not include cohabitation (503-7). Two persons of opposite sexes living in a stable union, whether legal or not, are called a couple (503-8). The term conjugal union (503-8) has been used by demographers to include both legal unions and more or less stable illegal unions.
 - 503-3  Concubinage, n.: a type of illegal union. A concubine in the restricted sense is a woman with an accepted conjugal status inferior to that of a legally recognized wife, particularly in polygynous societies. In other societies, the word concubine is sometimes used loosely to denote any woman other than a wife living in conjugal union with a man. Today such terms as companion or mate are preferred.
 - 503-7  Cohabitation, n.- cohabit, v.

terms.label: nuptiality rate

terms.context:
Relative marriage frequency is measured by marriage rates (520-1) or nuptiality rates (520-1), among which the crude marriage rate (520-2) gives the ratio of the total number of marriages to the total population in a given period. Male nuptiality (520-3) and female nuptiality (520-4) are often different, and can be studied separately. The terms male nuptiality and female nuptiality are used for the marriage frequency of the different sexes. A sex-specific marriage rate (520-5) can be computed with the appropriate population of each sex as a base. It is usual to distinguish between a first marriage rate (520-6), which relates the number of bachelors or spinsters (515-3 and 4) marrying to the total number of bachelors and spinsters respectively and a remarriage rate (520-7) which relates the number of remarriages to the total number of widowed and divorced persons. Similar rates can be computed by age or age-group of husband and wife whenever marriages are classified by age at marriage (520-8) of each spouse; such rates are called age-specific marriage rates (520-9). The tabulation of spouses by age at marriage permits the computation of the mean age at marriage (520-10) or average age at marriage (520-10) for the given year or period. Age differences between spouses (520-11) can be analyzed from a classification of the combined ages (520-12) of the spouses.

Cumulated marriage frequencies and cumulated first marriage frequencies are used in cohort studies.

terms.label: fertility
terms.gloss: Fertility refers to phenomena connected with human childbearing or reproduction.
terms.context:
Demographic studies of fertility (601-1) deal with certain phenomena connected with human childbearing (601-2) or reproduction (601-2). The term natality (601-1) is sometimes used instead of fertility. These terms refer to the frequency of occurrence of births (601-3) or more specifically live births (601-4) — within populations and sub-populations. A birth is the process of delivering a child. Live births or the births of live-born children (601-5) are distinguished from late foetal deaths (cf. 411-5) by evidence of life, such as respiration, movement of voluntary muscles or heartbeat of the child after complete expulsion or extraction. The term effective fertility (601-6), which was once used to indicate that late foetal deaths were not counted among the total number of births, should refer to the cases in which the deaths of infants or children are excluded from consideration. The term total fertility (601-7) has on occasions been used to refer to live births and late foetal deaths combined. The term differential fertility (601-8) designates fertility differences between the subgroups of a population.
 - 601-1  On the meaning of the term fertility in demography, see also § 623.
 - 601-2  Reproduction, n. - reproduce, v. - reproductive, adj. Frequently, reproduction refers to the balance of births and deaths (as in § 711) rather than to the process of childbearing or procreation.
 - 601-3  The word birth is now commonly used to mean live birth.
 - 601-4  Live-born, adj. also used as noun to mean: infant born alive.

terms.label: legitimacy

terms.label: multiparous
terms.gloss: Multiparous indicates a woman who has given birth more than once.
terms.context:
Births are also classified by birth order (611-1), e.g. first births, second births, etc. Birth order is usually determined by considering all previous births to the mother (611-3), and sometimes only births of the present marriage (611-2). Birth order is generally based on live births only, but occasionally late foetal deaths are taken into account as well. A classification of women by confinement order (611-4) is made in the same way as for births by counting all pregnancies which lasted at least 28 weeks, and reckoning multiple births as one confinement (cf. 603-4). Similarly a classification by pregnancy order (611-5) is made by counting all known pregnancies. In medical parlance, a woman is called nulligravida (611-6) if she has never been pregnant; the terms primigravida (611-7) and multigravida (611-8) respectively are used for a woman who is pregnant for the first time or who has been pregnant before. Women are also classified by parity (611-9), usually on the basis of the number of children born alive, although in biological literature the term refers to the number of confinements, and a woman who has had no confinement at all is said to be a nullipara (611-10) or nulliparous (611-10). Similarly, a woman is termed a primipara (611-11) and deemed to be primiparous (611-11) at her first confinement and a multipara (611-12) or multiparous (611-12) at subsequent confinements.

terms.label: secondary sterility
terms.gloss: A condition of sterility that arises after one or more children have been born.
terms.context:
The capacity of a man, a woman or a couple to produce a live child is called fecundity (621-1). The lack of that capacity is called infecundity (621-2) or sterility (621-2); inability to conceive (621-3) and inability to procreate (621-10) are the main, but not the single causes of sterility. Used alone, sterility usually carries the connotation of irreversibility, but occasionally temporary inability to conceive (621-4) and temporary sterility (621-5) are distinguished from permanent inability to conceive (621-6) and permanent sterility (621-7). Among women we distinguish primary sterility (621-8) where the woman has never been able to give birth, and secondary sterility (621-9), which arises after one or more children have been born.

 - 621-2  Sterility, n. - sterile, adj. Infecundity, n. - infecund, adj.

terms.label: sterile period
terms.gloss: Sterile periods are the times in each menstrual cycle when conception cannot occur.
terms.context:
The term temporary sterility (621-5) is used even in instances where a woman’s inability to conceive is not the result of a pathological condition.Women are said to have sterile periods (622-1) in each menstrual cycle (622-2), because generally conception can occur only during a few days around the time of ovulation (622-3). The period of sterility that extends from conception (602-1) to the return of ovulation after a delivery, which includes pregnancy (602-5) and is influenced by the duration of breastfeeding (622-4), is called the nonsusceptible period (622-5), particularly in mathematical models of reproduction. Temporary sterility is also used to refer to the occurrence of anovulatory cycles (622-6) (i.e., menstrual cycles in which ovulation does not occur) or to abnormal periods of amenorrhea. The sub-fecundity (622-7) of very young women is commonly called adolescent sterility (622-8); it would be better to talk about adolescent sub-fecundity (622-8).

terms.label: birth rate
terms.gloss: The birth rate is a rate calculated by relating the number of live births in a population during a given period to the size of that population.
terms.context:
The general term birth rate (632-1) refers to a rate calculated by relating the number of live births observed in a population or sub-population during a given period to the size of the population or sub-population during the period. The rate is usually stated per 1,000, and the most usual period is one year. Where the term birth rate is used without qualification, it is understood to be the crude birth rate (632-2), and all live births are related to the entire population. The total birth rate (632-3) based on live births and late foetal deaths is sometimes calculated. Marital birth rates (632-4) (legitimate birth rates (632-4)) and non-marital birth rates (632-5) (illegitimate birth rates (632-5)) are also calculated with legitimate and illegitimate births in the numerator and the currently married and unmarried female population, respectively, in the denominator. The illegitimacy ratio (632-6), the number of illegitimate births per 1,000 total births, is more frequently used, however. To compare the fertility of different populations, standardized birth rates (632-7) are often used to eliminate the effect on the birth rate of certain differences in structure of the population (most commonly the age and sex structure). The child-woman ratio (632-8), most commonly the number of children aged 0 to 4 per 1,000 women of childbearing age, e.g., 15 to 49, is used as an index of fertility when reliable birth statistics are not available.
 - 632-4  The denominator of the marital and non-marital birth rate is sometimes the total population.
 - 632-5  See note 4.

terms.label: standardized birth rate
terms.gloss: Standardized birth rates are used to compare fertility across different populations by eliminating the effects of population structure differences.
terms.context:
The general term birth rate (632-1) refers to a rate calculated by relating the number of live births observed in a population or sub-population during a given period to the size of the population or sub-population during the period. The rate is usually stated per 1,000, and the most usual period is one year. Where the term birth rate is used without qualification, it is understood to be the crude birth rate (632-2), and all live births are related to the entire population. The total birth rate (632-3) based on live births and late foetal deaths is sometimes calculated. Marital birth rates (632-4) (legitimate birth rates (632-4)) and non-marital birth rates (632-5) (illegitimate birth rates (632-5)) are also calculated with legitimate and illegitimate births in the numerator and the currently married and unmarried female population, respectively, in the denominator. The illegitimacy ratio (632-6), the number of illegitimate births per 1,000 total births, is more frequently used, however. To compare the fertility of different populations, standardized birth rates (632-7) are often used to eliminate the effect on the birth rate of certain differences in structure of the population (most commonly the age and sex structure). The child-woman ratio (632-8), most commonly the number of children aged 0 to 4 per 1,000 women of childbearing age, e.g., 15 to 49, is used as an index of fertility when reliable birth statistics are not available.

terms.label: fertility rate
terms.gloss: The fertility rate is a measure of the number of births per thousand individuals within a specific group, typically women of reproductive age.
terms.context:
The term fertility rate (633-1) is often used when the denominator of the birth rate is restricted to a group of individuals of the same sex in the reproductive ages (620-1). This denominator is commonly the mid-year population in the stated period, but it may also be the number of years lived by the group during the period, or the mean size of the group. Unless otherwise indicated, these rates are female fertility rates (633-2), and the rates are calculated for groups of women; the number of years lived by a given number of women in an interval is called the number of woman years (633-3). Male fertility rates (633-4) are computed sometimes in an analogous manner. Fertility rates are generally expressed as births per thousand (implied: individuals of the same category — sex, age, marital status, etc. — cf. 133-4). Marital fertility rates (633-5) or legitimate fertility rates (633-5) relate the total number of legitimate births (610-3) to the number of currently married women; non-marital fertility rates (633-6) or illegitimate fertility rates (633-6) relate the total number of illegitimate births (610-4) to the number of single, widowed and divorced women. Overall fertility rates (633-7) make no distinction according (610-1) to the marital status of the parents. The general fertility rate (633-8) relates the total number of births to all women of reproductive age regardless of marital status. Rates based on a narrower age range (usually one-year or five-year age groups) are called age-specific fertility rates (633-9) or age-specific birth rates (633-9).

 - 633-5  Marital fertility or legitimate fertility: the fertility of married persons (see 635-1).
 - 633-6  Non-marital fertility or illegitimate fertility: the fertility of unmarried persons.

terms.label: fertility history

terms.context:

Fertility histories are often obtained retrospectively from surveys. Family forms (638-1) are used in historical demography (102-1), where they are established for a married couple and its children by family reconstitution (638-2) on the basis of vital records (211-3). A woman’s pregnancy history (638-3) or pregnancy record (638-3) contains detailed information about her pregnancies including the date when each began and ended, and the outcome of the pregnancy. For example, they can provide information on natural fertility (638-4), i.e., fertility in the absence of family limitation (624-4). They are also used to estimate fecundability (638-5), the probability of conceiving per menstrual cycle (622-2). A distinction is made between natural fecundability (638-6), in the absence of contraception, and residual fecundability (638-7) in the opposite instance. The term effective fecundability (638-8) designates a fecundability that is reckoned in terms of conceptions that result in live births only. The conception rate (638-9) during the period of exposure to risk often estimated using the Pearl index (638-10) (613-1) is used to measure the effectiveness of contraception during periods of contraceptive use.

terms.label: fecundability
terms.gloss: Fecundability is the probability of conceiving during a menstrual cycle.
terms.context:
Fertility histories (638-1) or reproductive histories (638-1) are accounts obtained for individual women of the important events in their reproductive lives, such as marriages, pregnancies, births, infant deaths, etc., and their dates. Fertility histories are often obtained retrospectively from surveys. Family forms (638-1) are used in historical demography (102-1), where they are established for a married couple and its children by family reconstitution (638-2) on the basis of vital records (211-3). A woman’s pregnancy history (638-3) or pregnancy record (638-3) contains detailed information about her pregnancies including the date when each began and ended, and the outcome of the pregnancy. Such detailed records on the timing of fertility have been used for various purposes. For example, they can provide information on natural fertility (638-4), i.e., fertility in the absence of family limitation (624-4). They are also used to estimate fecundability (638-5), the probability of conceiving per menstrual cycle (622-2). A distinction is made between natural fecundability (638-6), in the absence of contraception, and residual fecundability (638-7) in the opposite instance. The term effective fecundability (638-8) designates a fecundability that is reckoned in terms of conceptions that result in live births only. The conception rate (638-9) during the period of exposure to risk often estimated using the Pearl index (638-10) (613-1) is used to measure the effectiveness of contraception during periods of contraceptive use.
 - 638-1  Birth histories are usually limited to live births.
 - 638-6  When used alone, the word fecundability stands for natural fecundability.

terms.label: period fertility
terms.gloss: Period fertility refers to the fertility of a specific year or period, calculated using age-specific fertility rates.
terms.context:
A summary index of period fertility (639-1), i.e., the fertility of a particular year or period, computed by the summation of the series of age-specific fertility rates constituting the fertility schedule (639-2) and representing a synthetic measure of fertility (639-3), is the total fertility rate (639-4) or total fertility (639-4). Other summary period indices can be obtained, such as the total marital fertility rate (639-5), the summation of marriage duration-specific fertility rates, and the order-specific total fertility rate (639-6), the summation of age-specific fertility rates order by order. The ratio of births to marriages (639-7) is computed by relating the number of births of a given year, either to the marriages of the year, or to a weighted average of the marriages of the current and of the preceding years.

 - 639-4  This is not a rate in the meaning of (133-4). Total fertility for a given year represents the number of children that would be bom per 1,000 women if they experienced no mortality and were subject to the age-specific fertility rates observed for that year. The period gross reproduction rate (see 711-4) which is derived by multiplying the total fertility rate by the proportion of female births, has often been used in the past, but the total fertility rate is preferred at present as the summary index of period fertility.

A summary index of period fertility (639-1), i.e., the fertility of a particular year or period, computed by the summation of the series of age-specific fertility rates constituting the fertility schedule (639-2) and representing a synthetic measure of fertility (639-3), is the total fertility rate (639-4) or total fertility (639-4). Other summary period indices can be obtained, such as the total marital fertility rate (639-5), the summation of marriage duration-specific fertility rates, and the order-specific total fertility rate (639-6), the summation of age-specific fertility rates order by order. The ratio of births to marriages (639-7) is computed by relating the number of births of a given year, either to the marriages of the year, or to a weighted average of the marriages of the current and of the preceding years.
 - 639-2  Also, fertility distribution or fertility function.
 - 639-4  This is not a rate in the meaning of (133-4). Total fertility for a given year represents the number of children that would be bom per 1,000 women if they experienced no mortality and were subject to the age-specific fertility rates observed for that year.  - 639-5  Or total marital fertility. The term is also used to describe the sum of the age-specific marital fertility rates above age 20.

terms.label: abortion rate
terms.gloss: The abortion rate is a measure of the frequency of abortion in a population during a given period, usually a year.
terms.context: Where induced abortion (604-2) has been legalized, it is possible to compile statistics on legal abortions (604-4). The abortion rate (640-1) is a measure of the frequency of abortion in a population during a given period, usually a year. Abortions may be related to the total population or to the number of women in the reproductive ages and may be specific for age, parity or any other characteristic. The abortion ratio (640-2) is a measure of the frequency of abortions in relation to the number of live births (601-4) during the same period. The life-time abortion rate (640-3) is the sum of age-specific abortion rates (640-4) and is a synthetic measure of abortion per woman or per 1000 women. These rates are the ratio of the number of abortions reported at each age to years lived by all women of the same age. If women can be classified according to their marital status, abortion rates by age and marital status (640-5) can be obtained. It is often also relevant to divide the number of abortions by the number of conceptions and so to calculate the probability that a pregnancy results in an abortion by age and marital status (640-6).

terms.label: growth rate

The ratio of natural increase (701-7) to the average population during a period is called the crude rate of natural increase (702-6) and is equal to the difference between the crude birth rate and the crude death rate. The vital index (702-7) is the ratio of the number of births to the number of deaths during a period; this measure is no longer much used.

terms.label: intrinsic rate of natural increase
terms.gloss: The intrinsic rate of natural increase is the constant annual rate of increase of a closed population subjected to constant age-specific fertility and mortality rates.
terms.context:
It can be shown that when a closed population (701-4) is subjected to constant age-specific fertility and mortality rates (631-8; 412-1) for a sufficiently long period of time, its annual rate of increase will tend to become constant. This constant rate of increase is called the intrinsic rate of natural increase (703-1), and a population which has reached this stage is called a stable population (703-2). The proportion of persons in different age groups in such a population will be constant, i.e., the population will have a stable age distribution (703-3). This stable age distribution is independent of the initial age distribution (703-4) and depends only on the fertility and mortality rates that are kept constant. Human populations never reach exact stability in practice, as fertility and mortality rates constantly change, but the computation of a stable population as a model and of its intrinsic rates may provide an index of the growth potential (703-5) of a set of age-specific fertility rates applied to a non stabilized age structure. Related to the growth potential, the moment of inertia of a population or demographic momentum (703-11) should be mentioned: it refers to the dynamics hidden in the age structure due to a delayed growth response caused by the biological fact that from the time of birth of a cohort (116-2) to the beginning of their period of fertility (620-1) a certain amount of time passes. A population may for this reason still grow, even though the birth rate drops long ago. The reverse case is also possible. The momentum is particularly altered in case of discontinuity in the evolution of births and abrupt reversals of trends. A stable population in which the intrinsic rate of natural increase is zero is called a stationary population (703-6). In such a population the numbers in a given age group are equal to the integral of the survivorship function (431-3) of the life table taken between the upper and lower age limits of the group, multiplied by a factor of proportionality common to all age groups. A quasi-stable population (703-7) is a formerly stable population with constant fertility and gradually changing mortality; characteristics of this type of population are similar to those of a semi-stable population (703-8) which is a closed population with a constant age structure. A logistic population (703-9) is a population growing in accordance with the logistic law (703-10) of growth, i.e., a population in which the growth rate decreases as a linear function of the population already alive and which will tend asymptotically to an upper limit. - 703-1 The intrinsic rate, also called by its inventor Lotka, the true rate of natural increase, is equal to the difference between the intrinsic birth rate (or stable birth rate) and the intrinsic death rate (or stable death rate). - 703-2 Stable, adj. - stability, n. - stabilize, v.
Stable population analysis uses the properties of stable population models to estimate various characteristics of real populations. - 703-6 Stationary, adj. - stationarity, n.

terms.label: gross reproduction rate

terms.label: population projection
terms.gloss: Population projections are calculations that show the future development of a population based on certain assumptions about fertility, mortality, and migration.
terms.context:
Population projections (720-1) are calculations which show the future development of a population when certain assumptions are made about the future course of population change, usually with respect to fertility, mortality and migration. They are in general purely formal calculations, developing the implications of the assumptions that are made. A population forecast (720-2) is a projection in which the assumptions are considered to yield a realistic picture of the probable future development of a population. Although the projection period (720-3) is variable, short-term forecasts (720-4) are the rule, as the margin of error to which forecasts are subject increases considerably as the length of the forecast’s period increases. The most frequently used method of projection is the component method (720-5) or cohort-component method (720-5) which takes the population distributed by age and sex at a base date (720-6) and carries it forward in time, cohort by cohort, on the basis of separate allowances for fertility, mortality and migration. When matrix algebra is used for component projections, the method is sometimes called matrix method of projection (720-7).
 - 720-1  Projections are also made in terms of educational, economic and social characteristics. Backward projections which might be more accurately called retrojections, use similar methods to trace the past evolution of the population.

The concept of migration is often not applied to moves made by persons without a fixed place of residence, for example, nomads are excluded from the count of migrants in many countries. In practice it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between migration, which implies a relatively permanent change of residence, and temporary moves (801-6), except on the basis of criteria of length of absence (801-7) from the place of origin or duration of stay (801-8) at the place of destination. In general, geographic mobility does not include short-term trips which involve no change of usual residence, even though such moves may deserve study because of their economic and social importance. Commuting (801-9) involves the daily or weekly journey from place of residence to place of work or schooling; seasonal moves (801-10) have a yearly periodicity. Transits (801-11), which are moves across a territory to reach a destination, do not involve migration with respect to the territory crossed. Tourist traffic (801-12) or vacationing (801-12) also are not included in geographic mobility.
